articles.content_orig:
Instead of adopting Washington’s security priorities, Canberra should leverage superpower rivalry to its own advantage, argues policy veteran John Edwards
Australia’s preparations for a possible conflict with China reflect “a relatively superficial understanding”, argues prominent economist John Edwards. Europe, Canada, Indonesia, Malaysia and India, he notes, are not preparing for such a conflict. Why should Australia?
Instead, he sees US-China rivalry as a potential advantage. Sitting between a security partner in Washington and a major economic partner in Beijing can underpin Australian prosperity for 25 years – provided Canberra does not pick sides.

articles.title_orig: Internal documents reveal scramble for funds before around-the-world "forever cruise" was stranded
articles.title_zh: Internal documents reveal scramble for funds before around-the-world "forever cruise" was stranded
articles.content_orig:
When the journey of the MV Odyssey luxury cruise ship came to a sudden end earlier this week in Cambodia, giving residents on the ship just hours to disembark, it marked the culmination of several attempts over a period of about three months to save the unique voyage.
According to accounts from multiple sources familiar with the final weeks on board, those included a scramble to find fuel while stuck at a port in Singapore, a rush by the crew to obtain provisions once food shipments had ended, and the temporary detainment of the ship in Hong Kong.
The voyage of the Odyssey, which is operated by Florida-based Villa Vie Residences, was billed as a continuous around-the-world cruise when it launched in October 2024. It allowed passengers to become residents of the ship by purchasing cabins for several hundred thousand dollars.
However, more than 200 passengers and dozens of crew members became stranded in Cambodia on Tuesday when Villa Vie suddenly suspended operations because of major financial issues .
In early August, the Odyssey was docked in Singapore when Villa Vie warned that the ship was at risk of being detained and the operator said it urgently needed to raise money.
"There's no question that we ran out of money in Singapore," said Darrell Carp, a Villa Vie resident who told CBS News he is out $250,000.
Multiple residents told CBS News they were concerned about giving money directly to the company because they believed the finances were being mismanaged by Villa Vie.
"We never fully understood the level of their debt," Carp said. "They were already behind on their payments on crew, and provisions, and fuel, and things like that."
A source close to the company said that when fuel prices spiked this year after the U.S. attacked Iran , it was a disaster for the company's business model.
After some passengers raised money while the ship was stuck in Singapore, $400,000 was paid to a fuel supplier directly out of one resident's personal checking account so the Odyssey could continue its journey, sources said.
At that time, Villa Vie was in the hole for several million dollars, according to internal documents reviewed by CBS News. Hundreds of thousands of dollars were owed to a port agent, fueling companies, food vendors and the crew.
Those internal documents showed that in a town hall on Aug. 4, residents were warned there was a real possibility of halting operations, laying off staff and repatriating the crew.
According to documents reviewed by CBS News, the ship was potentially days away from losing its insurance. It said that it would cut internet service to save money and was paying just enough to keep sailing.
In early August, Villa Vie introduced a so-called VIP "Villa Incentive Program" to help raise emergency funds, according to the documents. The VIP program was only open to current Villa Vie passengers so they could purchase more cabins at a discounted rate.
By Aug. 18, the company posted: "We have the commitment of over 20 cabins on the VIP sales!"
The program was initially an idea by the residents. Instead of just raising funds, it was designed to give passengers an even greater ownership stake in the ship, according to passengers and a source close to the company.
There was urgency to sell the cabins. The last slide of a PowerPoint presentation by Villa Vie on the VIP program read, "Funds are due today."
The VIP program was able to raise enough funds to keep the ship operating, but it continued to struggle, sources said.
A source with knowledge of the VIP program also said cabins aboard the Odyssey were still being sold to Villa Vie residents despite the company operating at a loss at that point.
According to one document, the ship's finances showed that even at full occupancy, it would operate at a $600,000 loss. Average monthly operating costs were $3.1 million, but revenue at 100% occupancy with everyone paying full fees would only have been $2.5 million, the document showed.
A source close to the company disputes the $3.1 million number and claims that the ship's monthly operating costs were under $1 million.
In August, 139 of 490 cabins were unsold, according to the documents.
When the ship reached Vietnam, crew members allegedly had to buy food from local grocery stores to feed passengers because the company owed money to a food vendor that would no longer deliver food, according to sources familiar with the situation.
According to one source, the ship's hotel director allegedly had to bribe local customs officials in Vietnam in order to get food onto the ship.
Later, in Hong Kong, court records obtained by CBS News showed the ship was detained until the company paid $167,844.48 to a fuel provider.
Villa Vie founder Mike Petterson has said skyrocketing fuel costs were what ultimately caused the ship's journey to come to an end.
When asked by CBS News Wednesday if creditors might seize the ship, Petterson told CBS News: "We will likely file for Chapter 11 here any day, right, which will put a stay on that while we go through the restructure process."
A source close to the company said Villa Vie stopped conducting cabin sales externally after Aug. 4, once the ship knew it was essentially out of money and needed to raise funds.
Yet on July 27, just a week before the ship ran out of money, Villa Vie had announced it was in the process of purchasing a second ship, the Legacy, and offered residents who were buying a cabin on the future ship an opportunity to take up immediate residency on the Odyssey.
A source close to the company said it was necessary to buy more ships to scale up for the business model to work.
This story published first on CBS News at 7:03 a.m. on Oct. 30, 2026.

articles.title_orig: Stock market today: Nasdaq dives over 3%, S&P 500 and Dow tank as AI reckoning grips Wall Street
articles.title_zh: Stock market today: Nasdaq dives over 3%, S&P 500 and Dow tank as AI reckoning grips Wall Street
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Google ’s share price has dramatically plunged amid a panic over AI .
Parent company Alphabet finished Thursday down more than 12 per cent, wiping $500 billion from its value. It represents the biggest ever crash in Google’s history, and second only among US listed companies to a $593 billion plunge in Nvidia’s value last year, after the rise of China’s DeepSeek AI brought concerns that US artificial intelligence companies could lose the race.
It comes after Alphabet’s latest results showed disappointing earnings in its search advertising business and the full scale of its vast spending on artificial intelligence . But shareholders are concerned that those huge bets may not come off, and that the company and the rest of the tech industry may not recover its investment in AI.
The results did show that Google is already earning from the AI boom, with revenues in its cloud business more than doubling. But investors are concerned that in the search business that still represents a large part of its earnings, Google is yet to see its embrace of AI results turning into profit.
Google and its chief executive Sundar Pichai have looked to aggressively embrace AI, after a relatively slow start against other companies such as OpenAI. It has begun to use its Gemini model to answer many search queries, for instance – despite the fact that advertising in search results has been a reliably huge business for parent company Alphabet.
"In a market ⁠worried about AI cannibalising the franchise, investors need to see search accelerating, not decelerating," said Dave Wagner, portfolio manager at Aptus Capital Advisors.
"Cloud is carrying the story, but until search shows AI is additive, the stock's probably going to trade lower."
The Mountain View, California company reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion, versus analyst expectations that it would come close to breaking even.
Aggressive efforts to boost cloud capacity and fund AI development led Alphabet to burn $5.9 billion last quarter, the first time it went into the negative in 22 years as a ⁠public company.
Total revenue missed Wall Street targets: revenue growth for Google Cloud outpaced expectations but was ​not enough ⁠to offset a $1.4-billion miss in advertising.
Alphabet's second straight quarter of negative cash flow was a sharp turn for a company that was long one of the tech sector's most prolific cash generators.
Moreover, Alphabet still plans to significantly increase its 2027 capital expenditures from this year's spending forecasts of $195 billion ⁠to $205 billion, Chief Financial Officer Anat Ashkenazi told analysts on a conference call.
While executives did not put a number on 2027 outlays, investors were nervous about ​a big jump.
"A $300-billion (capex) ⁠number could potentially scare the market because free cash flow now ‌is finally negative," said Jeremy Saltsburg, senior investment officer at Check Capital.
In contrast, rival Microsoft, which also reported results on Wednesday, saw shares rise more than 5%, fueled by positive free cash flow that outstripped analyst estimates.
Ashkenazi added that she expected near-term margin pressure from the use of third-party cloud capacity.
Net income available to ‌common Alphabet shareholders fell 25% to $26.17 billion, and adjusted earnings per share of $2.67 missed Wall Street targets ‌of $3.02.
The results reflect the huge costs of the AI buildout, with investors concerned both by potential overspending and the risk of falling behind rivals by not spending enough.
Total third-quarter revenue of $127.6 billion fell short of analysts' estimate of $128.2 billion, LSEG data showed. Revenue from ads came in at $82 billion, missing expectations of $83.4 billion.
Chief business officer Philipp Schindler attributed a larger-than-expected deceleration in search advertising growth to greater use of AI Mode, a chatbot interface ⁠for the search engine with which the company is still experimenting on ads.
Google would begin rolling out advertisements in AI Mode to international markets, Schindler told a conference call.
Alphabet attempted to offset the disappointing advertising performance by playing up its cloud computing unit, most notably by debuting Thomas Kurian, CEO of GoogleCloud, as a speaker on the earnings call.
Revenue at Google Cloud exceeded estimates and more than doubled to $30.71 billion in the third quarter ended September 30.
Kurian said sales of Google's tensor processing units (TPUs), which compete with Nvidia's GPU chips, had become a meaningful contributor to his business unit.
Alphabet started recognizing revenue from direct sales of what it called its "TPU Systems", spanning not only the chips but also associated hardware and software, last quarter.
But Ashkenazi cautioned that the buildout of TPU inventory would further place pressure on free ‌cash flow.
Google Cloud's backlog had grown to $561 billion and Alphabet expected to recognize more than 55% of it as revenue in the next 24 ​months, she added.
The third-largest cloud services provider globally after Amazon Web Services and Microsoft's Azure, Google Cloud has expanded enterprise commitments, supported by multi-year cloud and ‌AI infrastructure deals across cybersecurity, retail and financial services.
Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon, and ⁠Meta are projected to collectively spend well over $700 billion in 2026 to expand AI data center footprint, chips and high-performance networking capacity.
In the face of supply ⁠bottlenecks for advanced silicon and data center power, Alphabet's investments in custom tensor processing units alongside third-party GPUs have helped expand its service delivery capabilities.
Earlier on Wednesday, Google sought to preempt the results and counter a perception ‌of losing out in the AI race ​by unveiling the new Gemini 4 Carbon model.
This meant the company was again "leading at ‌the frontier," CEO Sundar Pichai said on the call.
Afterwards, analysts at Bernstein asked ​in a note, "Did Google rush the deployment of Gemini 4 models as an offset to softer financial metrics? And are the models ready for commercial deployment?"

articles.title_orig: China’s Fourth Aircraft Carrier Could Arrive as Soon as Next Year
articles.title_zh: China’s Fourth Aircraft Carrier Could Arrive as Soon as Next Year
articles.content_orig:
By ELINA SHIRAZI, US SENIOR POLITICAL REPORTER
Published: 13:43 EDT, 30 October 2026 | Updated: 18:12 EDT, 30 October 2026
A dramatic surge in military tension has taken center stage as President Trump ordered a third US aircraft carrier to the Middle East – all while making cryptic claims that the standoff will soon reach its conclusion.
US Central Command confirmed that bringing three aircraft carrier strike groups into the Middle East represents the largest US naval surge in the region since the 2003 invasion of Iraq .
Trump voiced confidence today that the conflict would dissipate, though he provided no specific timeline or strategy for how that outcome would be secured.
'It's going to get wrapped up soon,' Trump stated during an interview with a Kansas City radio station. 'We need a guarantee there'll never be a nuclear weapon.'
The remarks comes as questions surrounding Trump's domestic campaign itinerary arise, with the President rescheduling several canceled rallies over the weekend.
Vice President JD Vance also canceled a scheduled Friday press briefing in St. Cloud, Minnesota , focused on the administration's 'War on Fraud.'
Officials have not provided a reason for the cancellation.
Recent reports suggest the administration is laying the groundwork for a fresh wave of aggressive military strikes if Iranian leaders refuse to sign an agreement.
The aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln is pictured
During campaign appearances, he has argued that hostilities will wrap up shortly following the midterms, provided the GOP retains control of Congress
Despite initiating the war in February expecting a rapid surrender from Iran's weakened regime, Trump has continuously maintained that the conflict will draw to a close, even while combat intensifies and global economic damage continues to mount.
This has led to voter dissatisfaction across both parties ahead of the midterm elections.
During campaign appearances, he has argued that hostilities will wrap up shortly following the midterms, provided the GOP retains control of Congress.
Two US officials report that the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit are scheduled to arrive in the Middle East by late November.
Upon arrival, the Roosevelt will operate alongside the USS George H.W. Bush, which deployed in April, and the USS George Washington, which arrived in August as a replacement for the USS Abraham Lincoln.
Meanwhile, the nation's highest–ranking Middle East commander has reportedly briefed Trump on potential strike scenarios regarding Iran.
Admiral Brad Cooper visited the White House on Thursday with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and General Dan Caine, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the Wall Street Journal reports.
As Trump evaluates strategy options for resuming military action against Iran, the discussion with cabinet officials included potential plans for maintaining the ongoing regional blockade.
Following a high-level White House meeting involving military leadership and Vice President Vance, Hegseth removed Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia from his role as top strategist for the Joint Chiefs.
Sylvia's removal comes amid allegations that he leaked classified intelligence regarding the wars in Iran and Ukraine.

Polish president Karol Nawrocki turned back his plane en route to Senegal on Friday as the country’s top court was thrown into chaos after its president was suspended.
Police and protesters clashed outside the Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw after the government suspended its two senior justices and moved to bring criminal charges against them. Reports suggest riot police were deployed on Friday evening as demonstrators supporting the Law and Order (PiS) party, who oppose the government, threw objects at officers.
"At a moment like this, the President must be in Poland . I am cutting short my flight to Senegal. I am returning," Mr Nawrocki, who is backed by the PiS, said on X.
The tribunal ⁠said on its website that the court's president, Bogdan Swieczkowski, ​had ⁠been suspended on Friday.
A ‌long-running political dispute over the Constitutional Tribunal has effectively paralysed the institution.
Earlier this year, Mr Nawrocki, an ally of ‌Poland's former nationalist government of the Law ‌and Justice or PiS party, refused to swear in three of six judges nominated by parliament, while Swieczkowski, who was a deputy ⁠justice minister under PiS, declined to allow judges elected by the current parliamentary majority to assume their duties.
Restoring the rule of law is the government's duty, prime minister Donald Tusk said on X later on Friday.
“Restoring the rule of law is our obligation,” prime minister Tusk wrote on X on Friday evening. “After years of lawlessness under PiS this is a difficult process, sometimes painful and it requires decisive action. There is no other way.”
Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek told ‌reporters he has requested the ⁠lifting of the immunities of Swieczkowski and his deputy ⁠for failing to fulfill their duties by preventing judges from performing their ‌work.
PiS politicians, ​including leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski, said Tusk's ‌government was carrying out a ​coup on the tribunal.

articles.title_orig: Prominent Russian newspaper shuts down under pressure from authorities
articles.title_zh: Prominent Russian newspaper shuts down under pressure from authorities
articles.content_orig:
The Novaya Gazeta office building pictured on the day it announced its closure
At the editorial offices of Novaya Gazeta, they are packing up and shutting down.
Everywhere I look there are cardboard boxes and plastic bags. Everything must go.
For thirty years this has been Russia's most prominent independent newspaper, featuring investigative journalism fiercely critical of those in power.
Now Novaya Gazeta is being evicted from its home of three decades. The paper also says it's been blocked from receiving donations.
It's accusing the Russian authorities of killing it off.
"There are different ways to commit murder," journalist and co-founder of the paper Dmitry Muratov tells me. "They chose to strangle us."
"First, they blocked our websites and banned the paper edition. Then they revoked our media licence. One by one we were declared 'foreign agents', and our journalists were attacked.
"Now we can't earn any more money. The banks are refusing to accept donations from our readers. In our country there are political repressions going on. Those have reached us."
In 2021, Muratov was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for efforts "to safeguard freedom of expression, a precondition for democracy and lasting peace".
The award didn't stop the Russian authorities from designating him a 'foreign agent' in 2023. The label is often used to punish critics of the government.
Over the years Novaya Gazeta had developed a reputation for fearless investigative reporting on subjects such as corruption, human rights violations and abuse of power by officials and bureaucrats - dangerous topics in Russia.
The paper says that six colleagues were killed for "fulfilling their professional and civic duty". Those journalists include Anna Politkovskaya, who was shot dead in the stairwell of her apartment block twenty years ago this month. She had written extensively on the wars in Chechnya.
As I walk down a corridor, I spot the office Anna had used. Following her killing, the room and all the items in it were preserved and became a museum in her memory. Since the eviction order, most of the objects have already been removed. All that's left is the desk and, lying on top, a portrait of Anna.
In Novaya Gazeta's office, the room used by journalist Anna Politkovskaya, who was shot dead 20 years ago, had been left as it was when she was killed
In a statement on its website announcing the closure, Novaya Gazeta launched a stinging attack on the Russian authorities.
"They've killed us," it starts. "The newspaper is no more. The Russian authorities and Russian special services have forced the paper to stop its work."
The publication claims it is the victim of "a coordinated act" and blames "the repressive state apparatus".
"Human rights and freedoms have been eliminated in the country and their protection has been equated to a crimeâ¦ The courts have been destroyed along with the law. Having personal convictions is now state treason."
Journalists from Novaya Gazeta
Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the pressure on independent journalism and independent Russian journalists has been growing.
Soon after the start of what the Kremlin calls the 'special military operation', new laws were adopted in Russia. Their aim: to punish dissent and silence criticism of the war and of those in power.
Earlier this year there was a police search of Novaya Gazeta's editorial office. A veteran investigative journalist Oleg Roldugin was arrested and charged with "unlawful access to computerised information".
In connection with the case the newspaper's current editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov was recently taken in for police questioning and his home was searched.
Despite increasing pressure, Novaya Gazeta managed to continue operating, albeit in a reduced form. Loyal readers used VPNs, virtual private networks, to circumvent official blocking of the website. But the loss of its licence and other restrictions were a major blow to the publication.
How does Dmitry Muratov view the future?
"We are in the middle of a terrible catastrophe," Mr Muratov tells me. "Different dictatorships in the world seek chaos. They use chaos to rule their countries and peoples and to strengthen their personal power.
"I don't know what will happen next. I do know that we will do everything to stay true to our values: the human right to life. Human rights override the rights of states."
Novaya Gazeta's demise is very much the end of an era.
In an increasingly authoritarian Russia, it's also a sign of the times.
Putin can no longer claim victory in Ukraine, Nobel Peace Prize winner tells BBC

articles.title_orig: Wall Street closes sharply lower as AI cash burn fears spark tech selloff
articles.title_zh: Wall Street closes sharply lower as AI cash burn fears spark tech selloff
articles.content_orig:
By HUGO DUNCAN, BUSINESS EDITOR
Updated: 14:42 EDT, 30 October 2026
A Halloween slump in technology stocks has fuelled fears of a market crash that would hammer the savings and pensions of millions of British families.
On a brutal session in trading rooms in New York, the tech-heavy Nasdaq index followed up Thursday’s 1.4 per cent slide with a drop of more than 3 per cent on Friday.
Analysts warned of ‘tech carnage’ with shares in US giants Amazon and Intel among the biggest losers following bleak results on Thursday night.
Intel shares tumbled nearly 30 per cent – wiping around £90billion off its value – while Amazon fell more than 3 per cent.
The latest sell-off came after Google owner Alphabet tumbled more than 12 per cent on Thursday night – wiping close to £400billion off its value.
The tech titan, one of the so-called Magnificent Seven, is now down 30 per cent since its peak in May while the Nasdaq is off 7.5 per cent - wiping £2.5trillion off its value.
Traders are braced for turmoil on dealing floors around the world
A host of US tech stocks, driven to record highs this year on a wave of AI mania, are now in so-called ‘bear market’ territory – meaning they are down more than 20 per cent from their peak. Some have halved in value.
The FTSE 100 index has held up in the face of the sell-off – at least for now – as it benefits from a lack of exposure to tech and AI.
London’s blue-chip index closed up 7.71 points to 10,729.78 on Friday despite the ructions on Wall Street.
But the tech slump is proving painful for millions of British investors who are exposed to the US stock market through their pensions and Isas.
A host of Britain’s most popular investments, from technology funds and trusts and those that track major global indices, are packed full of US stocks now in reverse.
Neil Wilson, investor strategist at Saxo, warned of ‘tech carnage as October wraps up’ as investors fret over whether huge spending on AI infrastructure such as data centres will pay off.
He said: ‘This is starting to look quite ugly. The selloff looks a bit indiscriminate and shows that investors don't just want capex, they want to see the returns already.’
The AI trade has run into turbulence recently as investors grew uneasy about the billions Big Tech has poured into scaling up AI infrastructure while awaiting evidence of stronger returns.
Several companies have tapped the bond market to finance those investments, amplifying concerns that debt-funded spending will become harder to justify as borrowing costs rise.
Jake Behan, head of capital markets at Direxion, said the slump in share prices in recent days ‘is a good example of how the AI trade has changed’.
He added: ‘At this point, the market isn't just asking how fast you can grow. It's asking what you have to spend to get there.’
The AI trade got a brief respite earlier this week when AI lab Anthropic – which is behind the Claude model – unveiled plans to list on the US stock market with a value of up to £1.5trillion.
Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, said: ‘The FTSE 100’s lack of tech exposure has proved to be a blessing in disguise. The UK index is standing tall amid a global tech sell-off.'
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, described the slump in New York as an 'AI reality check'.
He said: ‘Investors are increasingly unhappy at the huge sums of money being spent on AI infrastructure without a clear roadmap for when, or whether, those investments will deliver a sufficient return. That means investors are questioning if money is being spent wisely.
'Big tech companies are going all-in with their bets that AI will be the biggest thing in decades to transform business and consumer life. If they get that bet wrong, the fallout could be huge.'
He added: 'Tech stocks have gone from being investors’ main feast to stale bread.
'For years, investors have treated tech as the golden ticket to wealth creation, and for a long time they have been richly rewarded. That enthusiasm is now evaporating, and some investors are racing for the exit.
'The gigantic declines we’ve seen this week in shares such as Alphabet and Intel suggest that investor sentiment has been turned on its head. Current price action implies tech investors want to jump off the treadmill rather than slow it down.'
The top ten holdings of the highly popular Vanguard FTSE All World ET highlight how much big US tech shares matter to UK investors
Millions of British savers are exposed to US tech stocks – even if they don’t know it.
Companies such as Nvidia, Alphabet, Apple, Meta, Amazon and Intel are held in countless global funds that form the backbone of pension savings.
When these stocks go south, so can the value of the nest eggs held by workers and pensioners alike.
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said: ‘The tech sell-off matters to investors around the world as the AI theme has weaved its way into countless sectors and geographies.
‘In particular, the US stock market is home to the giant tech names and is a major component of global funds that fill so many people’s investment portfolios.
‘This means that investors might find they have big tech exposure without realising it.’
He points out that 15 years ago, the US represented half of the MSCI World benchmark for the global stock market. It now stands at 73 per cent.
Tech is the dominant sector, making up more than 30 per cent of the index.
‘If tech goes off the boil, global funds might not provide the diversification support some investors expect,’ said Coatsworth.
For those who want to ‘dial down tech exposure’, he suggested switching into a global equity fund that excludes the US.
He pointed investors towards the iShares MSCI World ex-US ETF, which invests in a basket of companies from around the world excluding the US.
Tech stocks only account for 10.9 per cent of the portfolio, with financials the dominant sector at 27.9 per cent and industrials at 17.6 per cent.
‘The main holdings include banks, healthcare companies, oil producers and miners,’ said Coatsworth.
‘That would provide more sector balance and less dependence on tech, but it would mean some of the key names that have led the US market rally in recent years like Nvidia no longer being in the driving seat.’

Speaking about her closing message to voters, GOP Sen. Susan Collins said, "My final message to the people of Maine is to think about who can do more for Maine."
"If I am fortunate enough to be reelected, I will be fifth in seniority among the 100 senators. My opponent [Democrat Troy Jackson] would be either 100 or 99," she said while campaigning in Milo, Maine.
"And the fact is that seniority, relationships, knowledge and experience all really count in the Senate. They're the key to whether or not you're effective," she continued. "It has been 92 years since a Maine senator was chair of the Appropriations Committee. I feel that I've had a once-in-a-century opportunity to really deliver for Maine and for America."
Collins, who is seeking a sixth term in a blue-leaning state, has made her role atop the Senate Appropriations Committee central to her campaign, touting the federal funds that she has helped secure for projects in Maine.
The Justice Department's top prosecutor in Alaska called new reporting about the origins of an independent candidate's Senate campaign "troubling," and said the new information "has resulted in a significant surge of law enforcement assets" to the state.
But Michael Heyman, the U.S. attorney for the District of Alaska, declined to detail what specific crimes are being investigated as Daniel J. Sullivan, a candidate with the same first and last name as the Republican incumbent senator, Dan Sullivan, is set to appear on the ballot Tuesday. Heyman said he's "not making any assumptions on whether a crime has been committed or not."
"That's what we do, is we investigate whether a crime has been committed under several theories, so I'm not going to comment on what those theories are, and I'm also not going to put the cart before the horse," he said.
President Trump hedged his bets Friday when he talked about the midterms in the Oval Office.
"Tuesday, we're going to see how it all works out," he told reporters. "I think we're doing well. Typically, a president, whether he's good or bad, Republican or Democrat, loses the midterms. Nobody's ever explained why. But I think we have a shot at doing well, maybe very well, but you know, pretty well."
Speaking in the Oval Office with Stephen Hubbard , an American who was recently freed from a Russian prison, the president addressed the back and forth over whether he would hold in-person rallies in Kansas and Iowa.
"I wanted to see if I could do tele-rallies, because I'm very successful with — we're batting unbelievable at tele-rallies. I do them well, and it's a great instrument and it only seems to work for me because other people call and nobody gets on the phone," Mr. Trump said.
"I got a call from both states, Kansas and Iowa. We're in good shape, I think, in a lot of states. We had a great rally yesterday, as you know, for Darlene [Graham] in South Carolina. But I got a call from Iowa and from other people, and from my friends that are very, very good, and we have a couple of races that are very important. And they said, 'If you could go, it would be better than a tele-rally.' And I tried to talk them out of that. I said, what about a tele-rally? But they asked me, so I'm going to do two on Sunday."
The president said he would travel to Iowa first and then to Kansas.
"Monday is going to be exciting. But Sunday is going to be a very exciting day," he said. "And then Tuesday, we're going to see how it all works out. I think we're doing well."
Petersburg, Alaska — Daniel J. Sullivan, the independent candidate running for Senate in Alaska whose name is almost identical to the Republican senator running for reelection, left his hometown of Petersburg earlier this week, multiple sources confirmed to CBS News.
One resident and former student of Sullivan's said she saw Sullivan on a flight to Anchorage on Monday — two days before The New York Times first reported that he was recruited by operatives linked to Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign. The source added she did not know where Sullivan was headed, but another friend said he and his wife are known among friends as "world travelers."
Dozens of Petersburg residents also told CBS News they never saw or received any campaign materials like mailers, flyers, brochures or signs since the former elementary school teacher announced his candidacy last spring.
"I don't think it's a serious candidacy," said Andrew Worhatch, a Petersburg fisherman. "I haven't seen a platform."
The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals on Friday rejected the Justice Department's request for California to set aside disputed ballots received in the midterm election.
The panel's 2-1 ruling is the latest setback for the Trump administration's efforts to assert control over state-run elections.
The administration has alleged California sent ballots to some 20,000 people who may not be U.S. citizens. It wants the state to set those ballots aside and not count them until citizenship can be verified. California officials say the list is highly unreliable and likely includes many people who are U.S. citizens.
A district court judge already forcefully denied that request and warned that the Justice Department's demands could disenfranchise citizens.
"As the district court found — and we discern no clear error — there is no feasible way to identify and segregate the ballots of specific individuals without potentially catastrophic effects on the entire system," the appeals court wrote.
The Justice Department said in a court filing on Friday that it sent letters to all 50 states reminding them of their obligation to preserve election records for 22 months after an election.
The disclosure came in a filing in a suit brought by Democratic groups and officials over the Trump administration's efforts to pressure states to remove alleged ineligible voters from their rolls. District Judge James Boasberg in Washington, D.C., is overseeing the case. The judge had directed the DOJ and DHS after a hearing on Thursday to identify states where federal officials had sent communications since July 1, 2026.
The administration told the judge that federal agencies contacted election officials in five states about voters they identified as potentially ineligible.
The lawsuit, filed Oct. 20, was brought by the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, Democratic Governors Association, Nevada State Democratic Party, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries and a California voter.
The government confirmed it sent communications to California, Nevada, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Washington. (DHS contacted California, Nevada, Pennsylvania and New Jersey, while the Justice Department contacted California and Washington.)
The government said the July 16 letters to California, Nevada and Pennsylvania did not demand that states remove voters, withhold ballots or segregate ballots, but asked state officials to work with DHS to verify whether individuals identified through a preliminary analysis were noncitizens.

articles.title_orig: Binance loses $6.3 billion in crypto heist—what happens to your money when an exchange gets hacked
articles.title_zh: Binance loses $6.3 billion in crypto heist—what happens to your money when an exchange gets hacked
articles.content_orig:
A record-breaking hack at Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, is a reminder of the risks investors take when trusting a company to hold their digital tokens.
Binance said Friday that the security breach affected about $6.3 billion in client assets , making it the largest crypto hack on record. Around $3 billion of the affected assets has been frozen on blockchain networks, and the exchange says it has begun recovering some of them.
Binance's initial investigation suggests hackers gained access to the firm's withdrawal systems and were able to make unauthorized transfers from the exchange's crypto wallets, according to the company . The company says it has found no evidence that the private keys controlling those wallets were leaked and is still investigating the full scope of the breach.
The company says it will cover customers' losses . Binance maintains a roughly $1 billion emergency fund known as SAFU, which was created to protect customers in the event of a security breach. The company initially said SAFU and company funds would cover the losses, and has since said it has set aside more than $6.3 billion of its own funds.
For crypto investors, the Binance breach highlights one of the risks of keeping assets on an exchange. While exchanges make it easier to buy, sell and store crypto, what happens after a hack can vary widely, including whether customers get their money back.
Crypto exchange hacks aren't uncommon. Hackers stole roughly $1.5 billion from Dubai-based exchange Bybit in 2025, while Seychelles-registered Bitget lost more than $387 million in a hack in September 2026.
But a hack doesn't necessarily mean customers will lose their money permanently. Stolen assets can sometimes be recovered or frozen — preventing the hackers from moving or cashing them out — and exchanges may also have insurance, dedicated emergency funds or other company resources available to cover losses.
In Binance's case, roughly half of the affected assets have already been frozen, preventing some of the stolen crypto from being moved. Its roughly $1 billion SAFU emergency reserve provides another backstop, if needed.
Customers don't always recover stolen digital assets quickly. New Zealand exchange Cryptopia was forced into liquidation months after a 2019 hack in which about NZ$30 million in crypto was stolen. The liquidation process stretched on for years, with the first distributions finally beginning in 2024 .
"When you leave crypto on an exchange, you are relying on that company's controls and its balance sheet," says Martin Mulyadi, YHB Endowed Chair in Accounting and professor of accounting at Shenandoah University. "A pledge to make customers whole is only as strong as the resources behind it."
When considering where to transact in and hold crypto, start by researching the exchange itself. The Securities and Exchange Commission recommends searching for customer complaints and checking how the exchange is regulated.
U.S. customers can also check whether an exchange is registered with the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, or FinCEN, using its online database . Registration can help confirm that you're dealing with an identifiable business operating within the U.S. regulatory system, though FinCEN cautions that registration isn't an endorsement of the company.
Crypto experts also recommend reading an exchange's user agreement or terms of service. Some exchanges might have separate custody agreements or risk disclosures that are worth checking, too, Mulyadi says.
Look for language explaining who owns your crypto and what the exchange can do with it. Phrases such as "you retain title" or assets being "held for your benefit" are good signs, Mulyadi says. Check whether customer assets are kept separate from the exchange's own, which can offer extra protection if the company fails. And find out whether the exchange can lend or otherwise use your crypto, which can expose your assets to additional risk.
In the user agreement, check the exchange's limitation-of-liability section, Mulyadi says, and look at what insurance coverage the exchange offers and what it actually covers.
"If a refund after a hack is at the exchange's discretion, it's a goodwill gesture, not a promise," Mulyadi says.
Even strong language in the terms isn't a guarantee that your assets will be safe. FTX, the popular crypto exchange that collapsed in 2022, misappropriated billions of dollars in customer funds even though its terms said those assets belonged to customers, Mulyadi says.
If you don't want to hold your crypto through an exchange, there's another option known as "self-custody."
With self-custody, you use your own crypto wallet and control the private keys used to authorize transactions on the blockchain. Wallets typically come with a recovery phrase — essentially a master password that can be used to restore access to the wallet if you lose it.
That gives you control of your crypto without relying on an exchange, but it also makes you responsible for keeping that information safe.
And for anyone who's ever lost or forgotten a password, the risks of self-custody are real. With self-custody, there is "no help desk if you lose your recovery phrase," Mulyadi says.
For many investors, Mulyadi says a middle ground is keeping only what they actively trade on an exchange and holding longer-term assets themselves, as long as they understand how to safely store and recover them.
"Coins on an exchange are a promise from a company; coins in your own wallet are a responsibility you can't hand off," Mulyadi says.

articles.title_orig: iOS 27.2 adds two FaceTime features, including a personal favorite
articles.title_zh: iOS 27.2 adds two FaceTime features, including a personal favorite
articles.content_orig:
iOS 27.2 adds new features to Messages , Podcasts , Photos , and more—including some easy-to-miss upgrades to FaceTime. Here’s what’s new.
Dual Capture was added to FaceTime in iOS 27 and quickly became one of my favorite features. Rather than having to choose between showing your face or the rear camera view, Dual Capture lets you show both at once.
iOS 27.2 expands Dual Capture to work on all video calls, even with groups. Previously the feature was limited to one-on-one calls.
If you have an iPhone 17 or newer, all you have to do on a video call is hit the ‘Flip’ button, and by default both the front and back camera will be activated.
It’s a huge upgrade to the FaceTime experience, and especially great if, like in my case, you have young kids running around and want to let grandparents see them and you at the same time.
The only drawback: everyone in the call needs to have iOS 27, iPadOS 27, or macOS 27 installed.
iOS 27.2 makes FaceTime more accessible by adding support for third-party sign language interpreters and live captioning.
Inside the three-dot icon, you’ll find a ‘Sign Language’ button that lets you pick an installed VRS (Video Relay Service) app for direct access to an interpreter. The app will appear as a participant tile in the call with a “Waiting for Interpreter” status, then your interpreter’s name will display after they join.
For third-party live captioning, Apple has a step-by-step support document here that outlines the process. You can also optionally stick with the existing built-in Live Captions feature to have your iPhone add automatic captions. It’s available from Settings ⇾ Apps ⇾ FaceTime ⇾ Live Captions.
If you have an iPhone Duo, iOS 27.2 also introduced a new Edge Light feature that works across multiple video calling apps, including FaceTime.
Edge Light works just like on the Mac , adding a ring of light around the iPhone Duo display to better illuminate your face on calls. It’s a built-in alternative to using a physical ring light.
To enable the feature, open Control Center while on a FaceTime call then hit ‘FaceTime Controls’ and tap ‘Edge Light.’ Once enabled, you can adjust settings like the intensity and color temperature.
Have you tried any of iOS 27.2’s new FaceTime features? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title_orig: ‘Asleep at the wheel’: Wallace slams Trump over China spy report involving Nvidia CEO
articles.title_zh: ‘Asleep at the wheel’: Wallace slams Trump over China spy report involving Nvidia CEO
articles.content_orig:
Wallace shared “shocking” new reporting that she said may show Trump is “setting America up to be a great loser on the world stage.”
MS NOW’s Nicolle Wallace shared “shocking” new reporting from The New York Times, which she said could show that President Donald Trump is “asleep at the wheel in protecting U.S. national security.”
On Thursday’s “Deadline: White House,” Wallace discussed the Times’ “blockbuster” report about a Chinese businesswoman’s close relationship with Jensen Huang , president and CEO of Nvidia, the world’s most dominant leader in artificial intelligence chips. U.S. officials concluded the woman was a Chinese intelligence asset, according to the report.
“The discovery that Beijing was getting reports from someone with direct access to Mr. Huang, one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. revolution as well as an influential ally of President Trump’s, set off alarms at the White House,” the Times reported.
“What happened next,” Wallace said, “is the stuff of international political scandals.” The Times said Trump was briefed on the intelligence findings but chose not to act. He had “been wary of disrupting Nvidia’s chip sales, which are helping to drive the economy and the stock market, and of further complicating the trading relationship with China,” the report read.
“Donald Trump — the man who claims that no one is tougher on China than he is — does nothing,” Wallace said of the president’s reported inaction. She described “panic among our intelligence agencies as Trump sat by as a Chinese spy got dangerously close to the CEO of America’s most valuable company.”
Nvidia denied that its CEO had been targeted in a spy plot. The company told the Times that “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected” and that he “talks with thousands of customer executives every year.” The White House, the CIA and the National Security Agency declined to comment, according to the Times.
Wallace also pointed to “close financial ties” between Trump and Nvidia that were described in the report. A person familiar with the matter told the Times that Nvidia donated at least $20 million to Trump’s White House ballroom fund. Earlier this month, Trump disclosed that he bought up to $1.6 million worth of Nvidia stock and sold up to $1 million in August.
Wallace said the report exposed a gap between Trump’s public statements and private behavior.
“Earlier this year, he cited the importance of protecting America’s technological secrets and beating China in the AI arms race as his entire rationale for why AI can’t and should not be regulated ever,” she said.
By that logic, Wallace said, Trump is “setting America up to be a great loser on the world stage, as he imperils U.S. national security in a matter that’s deeply entangled in his own bottom line.”
You can watch Wallace’s full comments in the clip at the top of the page.

articles.title_orig: Outcry prompts ‘Call of Duty’ to cut Seoul tragedy footage
articles.title_zh: Outcry prompts ‘Call of Duty’ to cut Seoul tragedy footage
articles.content_orig:
American video game publisher Activision said Friday that it was removing controversial footage from its newly released “Call of Duty” game after an outcry in South Korea over the inclusion of real-life footage from a deadly 2022 Halloween crowd crush in Seoul.
Last week’s global release of “Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4” came days before the Oct. 29 anniversary of the disaster in the South Korean capital’s nightlife district of Itaewon, where a crowd of tens of thousands of partygoers surged beyond control in a narrow alley, causing nearly 160 deaths.
The game, which takes place amid a fictional North Korean invasion of the South, features about 10 seconds of heavily edited footage of the tragedy to illustrate what the aftermath of a Pyongyang attack might look like, though it does not refer to the Itaewon crowd crush directly.
Groups representing families of the crowd crush victims had demanded that the footage be removed, saying it was appalling that the game had directly reproduced actual scenes of people performing CPR “while victims lay on the cold streets amid chaos and desperation.”
“If the game developer has even the slightest sense of respect and empathy for the victims of the Itaewon disaster, it should promptly take corrective action,” the Itaewon Disaster Bereaved Families Association and Itaewon Disaster Citizens’ Countermeasures Committee said in a joint statement Friday.
The California-based game publisher, Activision, apologized in a statement and said the footage would be completely removed through a game update scheduled for release Nov. 12.
“This game is a fictional work created to provide a realistic and immersive experience,” the company said, according to the South Korean public broadcaster MBC. “In using actual news footage in the game, we never intended to evoke any tragic incident, including the Itaewon disaster, or to trivialize the suffering associated with such tragedies.”
The controversy came as grieving families are still waiting for answers about authorities’ failure to prevent the disaster four years ago. Nearly two dozen officials have been charged in the investigation, which is still underway, while three former police officers have been jailed.
On Thursday, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung vowed that his government would “uncover the truth.”
“On that day, when what should have been a joyful autumn night turned into the scene of a horrific tragedy, the state was nowhere to be found,” he said in a statement on X.
Lee Jin Woo, whose younger sister was 28 when she died in the crowd crush, told NBC News that he had played the new “Call of Duty” game and didn’t notice the Itaewon footage at first.
“But after hearing about it and thinking it over, I began to realize the footage looked very similar,” said Lee, who works at a South Korean gaming company.
“The more I thought about it, the more I felt betrayed as a gamer,” he said. “After all, it was a game company and a game series that I had liked.”
The game’s premise, in which South Korean conscripts are thrust into defending their country alongside American soldiers after a North Korean invasion, has been controversial since before it was available to play.
Though the “Call of Duty” invasion is fictional, it draws on North Korea’s real-life capture of Seoul in 1950 during the Korean War. The conflict ended in 1953 with an armistice instead of a peace treaty, and the two Koreas remain technically at war.
Tensions between the North and South have escalated in recent weeks, with the two countries embroiled in a standoff along their heavily militarized border. North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has rebuffed diplomatic outreach from Washington and Seoul as he continues to advance his nuclear and ballistic missile programs.
“Ultimately, whether we’re talking about an actual war or the Itaewon disaster, both involve the suffering of real people,” Lee Mi Hyun, a director at the Itaewon Disaster Citizens’ Countermeasures Committee, told NBC News in an interview.
“They’re turning that suffering into entertainment,” she said. “It’s an approach that seems to show absolutely no empathy for the people who experienced that suffering.”
Some South Korean lawmakers say the game should be taken as a warning.
“We need to pay attention to the question it raises,” Han Dong-hoon, an opposition legislator, said last week in a Facebook post. “If that day were to come again, would we be ‘prepared’?”
The game has also been defended by members of Lee’s governing Democratic Party such as Kim Han Kyu, who said there was “nothing wrong with playing a game set against the backdrop of North Korea’s nuclear weapons.”
“We are still technically under an armistice, aren’t we?” he said Thursday in a Facebook post. “Wouldn’t it be even stranger if no games depicted a war against North Korea?”
Others have used the game to criticize Lee’s conciliatory approach to North Korea, with opposition lawmaker Ahn Cheol Soo suggesting last week that the South Korean president try playing the game to correct his “naïve judgment” about the North Korean threat.
With its “Call of Duty” franchise struggling to sustain interest in recent years, the Microsoft-owned Activision used “Modern Warfare 4” to deliver what fans loved about its previous games: a hyperrealistic military shooter.
“I don’t think we were happy with every aspect of last year’s game, and we heard the feedback loud and clear,” Activision Chief Marketing Officer Tyler Bahl told “The Game Business Show” earlier this month .
“With ‘Modern Warfare 4,’ we’ve tried to adjust based on that feedback. It’s getting back to a grounded military shooter. Making it cinematic, making it authentic and bringing that edge back that ‘Call of Duty’ is known for,” he said.
That approach appears to have worked. As of Friday, “Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4” was the top-selling game in both South Korea and the United States on Steam , an online PC game distribution platform.
In its review, gaming website IGN said it was a “much-needed reminder of what ‘Call of Duty’ can be at its best, even if it can’t fully recapture the heights of its glory days.”
Mithil Aggarwal is a Hong Kong-based reporter/producer for NBC News.
Stella Kim is an NBC News freelance producer based in Seoul.

articles.title_orig: ExxonMobil and Chevron report blowout profits as Trump touts benefits of high oil prices
articles.title_zh: ExxonMobil and Chevron report blowout profits as Trump touts benefits of high oil prices
articles.content_orig:
It’s a good time to be an oil company.
The two largest U.S. oil companies, ExxonMobil and Chevron, on Friday reported blowout profits that easily beat expectations as oil prices remain sharply elevated because of the U.S. war with Iran.
ExxonMobil reported a profit that doubled from the same period last year, while Chevron’s earnings surged more than 180% from a year earlier.
As part of the bumper returns, Exxon said it was increasing the dividend it pays to investors.
The returns at both companies came as the price of oil surged beyond $100 per barrel and has remained there for months. On Friday, prices accelerated again, with Brent oil trading closing just under $118 per barrel.
The highest level that Brent reached since the United States and Israel launched the Iran war in late February was $126, which it is now approaching again.
Since the start of the year, Exxon shares have risen 52%, and Chevron shares have returned 50%.
Overnight, another major oil company, BP, reported that its profit skyrocketed to an 18-year high.
The average price of regular gasoline has soared 40% for consumers since the war broke out. Soaring prices continue to pressure consumers ahead of the midterm elections, where voters have repeatedly said that prices and inflation are primary concerns.
In 2024, Donald Trump repeatedly pledged to drive energy costs down . “My plan will cut energy prices in half or more than that within 12 months of taking office,” the then-candidate said in September 2024, while adding that it would mean “gasoline below $2 a gallon.”
As of Friday, the average gasoline price is currently more than double that.
In recent rallies on the campaign trail, the president has celebrated the higher oil and gas profits. “I wonder if I should say this,” Trump mused aloud during a rally Oct. 24, before saying “our country is making hundreds of billions of dollars because of what’s happened in the Middle East.”
Trump touts U.S. oil business making ‘hundreds of billions’
“My people said, ‘Please don’t mention that, sir,’ because people are paying a little higher,” Trump continued. “But what we’ve done for this country, we’re making money like this country has never made before.”
“I don’t give a damn: I’m going to say it. We’re making a freaking fortune.”
The higher prices are also a result of the war between Ukraine and Russia following President Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion of his neighbor in 2022.
“There’s a lot of disruption happening in the world,” ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods told CNBC on Friday morning . “What you’re finding is because of the closure” in the Strait of Hormuz, “shipping has to find new routes around to continue to deliver the products that society desperately needs.”
“About half of Russia’s refinery capacity has been taken out from the Ukraine bombing,” he added.
“That shortage of refining capacity and availability to the world is what’s driving product prices as high as it is, and frankly, diesel is the key crunch point here because it is so critical to economic growth,” Woods continued.
Since the start of the year, the average nationwide price for diesel fuel has risen 78%. New York-traded diesel futures have soared 130% since the start of the year, likely indicating more price rises could still come at the pump.
Both Exxon and Chevron said that they were running their refineries at maximum output to continue making as much diesel as possible.
Trump has taken specific note of the impact that diesel could have on the economy. The administration has quickly issued multiple orders and policies in an attempt to bring prices down.
The president signed an order allowing more widespread use of an off-road dyed variety of diesel, has pressured European allies to release more of the diesel reserves into the global market, and has announced a deal with Putin for some of that country’s diesel supplies.
Trump’s latest move came last week, when he announced $150 million in Defense Production Act funding to “expand petroleum production, storage, and logistics at refineries across.”
The moves have not meaningfully brought prices down.
On Friday, Woods said his refineries were already being pushed to the limit. “We are at record levels of utilization for our refineries,” he said on CNBC.
“If you look at North America, we produce record volumes of diesel. That’s all been a function of trying to drive more product into the marketplace to meet that demand and to drive costs down.”
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: Pakistan army ‘cautiously optimistic’ about US-Iran mediation efforts
articles.title_zh: Pakistan army ‘cautiously optimistic’ about US-Iran mediation efforts
articles.content_orig:
Pakistan’s army is “cautiously optimistic” ⁠about mediation efforts between Iran and the United States as regional countries seek to revive a ceasefire in the eight-month-old war.
Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, spokesman for Pakistan’s military, suggested on Friday that there were positive signs in attempts to de-escalate the conflict. His comments to the Reuters news agency were the first since a high-level delegation visited Tehran this week.
Army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, Pakistan’s chief mediator, has been to Tehran twice this month, most recently on Monday, alongside Saudi and Turkish officials.
“Why would the Field Marshal be going twice if it is not for some positivity? So yes, of course,” Chaudhry said when asked whether the trips were a positive ⁠sign.
“The word that we would use is always cautiously optimistic,” added Chaudhry, director general of Inter-Services Public Relations.
He also warned that there are parties seeking to obstruct mediation between the US and Iran.
There are still “powerful spoilers and detractors” who believe conflict serves them, he added without naming them.
Speaking in the garrison city of Rawalpindi, where Pakistan’s armed forces are headquartered, Chaudhry declined to say what was discussed in Tehran or whether the US had backed the trip.
His comments on Friday came as Qatari mediators arrived in Tehran in another apparent bid to negotiate a revival of the June ceasefire that collapsed months later.
Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin joined Pakistan’s Munir in ‌Tehran on Monday.
Their two countries signed a joint defence pact with Pakistan on August 7, saying an attack on any signatory will be treated as an attack on all.
The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement has taken on added significance as the Iran war has redrawn regional alliances and raised fears of a broader Middle East conflict.
While the three signatories say the agreement is aimed at collective deterrence and regional security, analysts see its evolution as closely tied to efforts by regional powers to manage the fallout from the Iran-US confrontation.
After Monday’s talks, Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said regional security should be ensured by regional countries without foreign intervention.
The wording of the pact does not bar new ⁠members, Chaudhry said on Friday when asked whether Iran could join.
“Anyone who has a shared vision of collective deterrence ⁠and regional peace, why not? Everyone is most welcome,” he said, adding that it was for the political leadership of the three principal parties to decide.
Asked whether more Pakistani troops were being sent to Saudi Arabia under the agreement, Chaudhry said that would depend on the situation and the decision of both countries’ political leadership.
He said Pakistan was committed to defending Saudi ⁠Arabia and the holy sites of Mecca and Medina. “We are not part of the Yemeni conflict, which is an intra-Yemen conflict,” he added.
Fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi group has been reignited by the Iran ⁠conflict, stoking fears of a wider war.

Watch the full series of Arkanaut on Warhammer TV now
The third and final instalment of the new Warhammer Age of Sigmar animation Arkanaut is live now, and available to watch on Warhammer TV . Warhammer+ subscribers can stream it at their leisure. If you’re not signed up yet, check out this trailer to see what you’re missing:
This video is hosted on a third party website, which may be using cookies. To see it, you need to accept cookies by clicking on the button below. You can change your preferences at any time by clicking Cookie Settings at the bottom of any Warhammer Community page.
Warning – if you’ve not watched the first two episodes yet, there are spoilers ahead!
Episode 3 opens with the remaining Arkanauts at the mercy of a new adversary – a Helsmith of the Fallen Ancestor Hashut. This first animated view of the Bullfather’s followers gives us a glimpse at just how divergent this culture is from their Kharadron cousins, and specifically, their perspective on power and technology.
The Kharadron Overlords and the Helsmiths of Hashut have a common lineage in the Khazalid empire of old – a culture that still endures relatively unchanged as the Khazalite Holds . The technology of their ancestors revolved around runes and the innate resonant magic of stone.
Both the Kharadron and the Helsmiths have since abandoned this technology. The Kharadron as there are not many rocks kicking about in the sky, and the Helsmiths as “harmony with nature” is not really how they roll.
Kharadron technology revolves around the use of a lighter-than-air material called Aether-gold, also called “the Breath of Grungni”. This powers not only their airships, but also their suits, weapons, and cities. In fact, without it, the entire Kharadron civilisation would quite literally come crashing to the ground. So the Kharadron dedicate much of their efforts to the finding and extraction of this valuable resource.
The Helsmiths have harnessed an altogether more dangerous material. Their technology runs on the distilled soul-essence of captured and processed daemons. As you might imagine, this is a volatile and unpredictable energy source, but incredibly powerful.
The Helsmiths believe that they are untainted by the use of this power, and that they have the willpower and fortitude to endure contact with this Chaotic essence. Their malevolent demeanor, sprouting tusks, and the fact that many of their most prolific magic users slowly petrify with use of this magical power source is entirely unrelated, probably.
This daemonic essence powers vast forges, which have become the greatest engines of industry in the Mortal Realms. These create vast arsenals of weapons and constructs for the Helsmiths and their dubious allies, taint the land about them, and drive the forced evacuation of other local denizens like skaven, orruks, and Gloomspite Gitz.
The forge in Arkanaut is a recently repurposed duardin hold that the Helsmiths have claimed and desecrated (as they see it, they’ve just retaken a piece of their ancestral heritage and put it to use again). There are some great shots of the forge in this episode, inspired by the custom scenery created to accompany the recent Helsmiths of Hashut battletome .
There is one more power source at play in this episode, of course.
In episode 1 , the Arkanauts harpooned themselves a Stormcast soul and trapped it inside a jury-rigged aether-tank, intending to sell it back to its brethren at a fair and reasonable price (or possibly another party at a less reasonable price, depending on market conditions).
Now the Helsmiths have the soul and we’re fairly sure they aren’t planning to use it for anything good…

articles.title_orig: Anthropic appears to have ordered AI tool Claude to stop remaking video games
articles.title_zh: Anthropic appears to have ordered AI tool Claude to stop remaking video games
articles.content_orig:
Update: Anthropic has confirmed it's released an update to Opus 5.5 to "steer" Claude Code away from "recreating someone else's specific game."
It appears Anthropic may be (quietly) taking action to stem the flood of AI-driven game remakes that have hit the video game industry in the last few month, which saw users creating their own versions of classic and upcoming games, sometimes for fun, sometimes for financial gain.
Earlier today X (formerly Twitter) user Chasm said that they spotted an update to Claude Code's "rules" that was pushed sometime on October 27. The rule is listed under "tengu_heron_brook," and reads "Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Do not build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original." Chasm reports that there is no way to disable the rule.
An Anthropic spokesperson referred us to a statement by Anthropic member of technical staff Addy Osmani also posted on X. "We added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy," Osmani wrote. "Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working. We'll continue to iterate to ensure we're striking the right balance."
Related: GDC Side Quest - An anti-cheat primer with Lucia Suarez
"In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that's yours, send it my way."
Fear over the potential of fast-follow AI remakes that might beat the copied game to market has spread among independent developers in the last few weeks. Digital Sun Games is one of several studios to cancel their upcoming public playtest for fear someone might ingest the demo into an AI tool and release their own version of its upcoming game ReVamp . Developers have also pressed Valve to explain how it can prevent the shady clones from supplanting their games on Steam, prompting the company to offer a rare explanation to developers in South Korea earlier in this week .
While developers may take some relief that Anthropic at least doesn't want to actively encourage mass game copying, this rule may only deter the most low-effort copycats. Scientists and reporters have repeatedly documented that safety limits on generative AI tools can be sidestepped by deploying rhetorical tricks . It's also unclear how the software would be able to interpret whether or not a user owns a game idea or game assets.
And as many users responding to Chasm pointed out, if Claude becomes too difficult to use, vibe-coding cloners can turn to open-weight models that have no such restrictions in place.
GameDeveloper.com has reached out to Anthropic for comment and will update this story upon its response.
Related: Epic VP says AI code tools have stomped out decade-old 'non-deterministic cooking bugs' in Unreal Engine
Update 10/30: This story has been updated with confirmation from Anthropic.
Senior Editor, GameDeveloper.com

His credits include Proxy Studios' 4X strategy game Zephon, Iron Anchor Studios' Down With The Ship, and Amplitude Studio's 2017 game Endless Space 2.

articles.title_orig: Oil giants post billions in profits as Americans feel pain at the pump
articles.title_zh: Oil giants post billions in profits as Americans feel pain at the pump
articles.content_orig:
Media coverage of the economy overemphasizes gasoline prices while ignoring a robust consumer spending boom, according to Larry Kudlow. He points out that consumer spending is growing at 3.5% after inflation.
U.S. oil giants raked in billions of dollars in profits in the third quarter as oil prices surged amid supply constraints caused by conflicts around the world, contributing to higher prices at the pump for consumers.
ExxonMobil, the largest U.S. oil producer by market capitalization, reported having more revenue from refining operations than from its exploration and drilling operations for the first time in at least six years.
Chevron's third-quarter downstream earnings also reached their highest point over the same timeframe.
The surge in revenue for the oil giants comes as Americans are facing higher prices at the gasoline pump, as the war in Iran's disruption of oil flows from the Middle East and the war between Russia and Ukraine has led to the targeting of energy infrastructure.
TRUCKING INDUSTRY HIT BY STRING OF BANKRUPTCY FILINGS AS DIESEL COSTS SURGE
American consumers have faced a significant uptick in gas prices this year, with prices surging above $4 a gallon nationally at times, according to AAA data.
AAA data showed that the national average price of a gallon of regular gas was $4.20 a gallon on Friday, down slightly from $4.43 a month ago but well above the average of $3.03 a gallon a year ago.
Diesel prices also reached their highest recorded average price last month, when they reached $6.52 a gallon on Sept. 22, AAA found.
Diesel costs are particularly significant for the trucking industry, and those costs can affect the price paid by consumers for groceries and other goods that are transported to stores around the country.
REPUBLICANS COULD FEEL 'SAME FATE' AS DEMOCRATS AS GAS PRICES ARE ELEVATED AHEAD OF MIDTERMS, EXPERT SAYS
American consumers have faced pain at the pump due to higher oil and gas prices. (M. Scott Brauer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Recent data from the Labor Department also reflects the surge in gas prices that Americans have faced over the past year.
The September consumer price index (CPI) released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics found that gas prices surged 9.1% on a monthly basis and were up 34.2% from a year ago.
ENERGY CEO SAYS AMERICANS AREN'T BENEFITING FROM LOW PRICES BECAUSE OF ONE MAJOR ROADBLOCK
The war in Iran has disrupted energy supplies this year, contributing to higher prices at the pump. (Giuseppe Cacace/AFP via Getty Images)
Gas prices have undergone significant shifts since the Iran war began in late February, with the BLS data showing monthly swings to the upside of 21.2% in March, 5.4% in April and 7% in May.
A cooldown in the conflict over the summer allowed gas prices to decline on a monthly basis by 9.7% in June and 2.9% in July.
However, concerns over the prospect of a resumption of hostilities and the impact on energy supplies caused prices to rise again in the last two months, with prices up 3.9% in August and 9.1% in September, per the BLS data.

articles.title_orig: Police Investigate Former Prince Andrew and Epstein’s Time at Balmoral, Royal Estate in Scotland
articles.title_zh: Police Investigate Former Prince Andrew and Epstein’s Time at Balmoral, Royal Estate in Scotland
articles.content_orig:
Kim Aris says ‘hearing her voice again means more than words can express’ amid loosening of detention restrictions
The son of Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi has been allowed to speak to the detained former democratic leader for the first time in more than five years.
“Today, I was finally able to speak with my mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, after more than five years. Hearing her voice again means more than words can express,” Kim Aris said in a post on Facebook on Thursday.
Aung San Suu Kyi is under house arrest in the capital, Naypyidaw, according to Myanmar authorities, where she has been sequestered since being unseated in a 2021 military coup .
Images accompanying his Facebook post appeared to show Aris, who lives in the UK, standing outside the Myanmar embassy in London.
“I am deeply grateful to everyone who has stood by my mother and me. I believe your voices helped make this moment possible,” he said in the post. “But my mother is 81 and remains unjustly detained. One conversation is not regular family access.”
Myanmar’s military has held the Nobel peace prize laureate in almost total seclusion since the February 2021 coup, which ended a tentative decade-long experiment with democracy. But in recent months authorities have increasingly advertised the loosening of her detention and published photographs of her taking private meetings, as supporters have demanded “proof of life”.
On Monday, authorities said she received a package from Britain’s King Charles, including two books about soil and a “sealed diplomatic communication” from the monarch. Buckingham Palace did not comment on the contents of the communication.
Myanmar authorities said Aung San Suu Kyi was moved from a prison in Naypyidaw to house arrest in April, and in August they published images of her meeting the nation’s Red Cross representative.
After ruling Myanmar as military chief since the coup, Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president this year.
Analysts described the election that put him in office as a charade, and said he could be loosening restrictions on Aung San Suu Kyi in an attempt to court international legitimacy.

articles.title_orig: Toyota reveals five new lifted Woodland concepts, including the bZ electric SUV
articles.title_zh: Toyota reveals five new lifted Woodland concepts, including the bZ electric SUV
articles.content_orig:
Toyota introduced a new family of lifted, “adventure-ready” Woodland concepts based on the RAV4, Grand Highlander, Sienna, Crown Signia, and bZ electric SUV.
Toyota is the latest automaker to chase the highly profitable off-road market in the US, with plans to expand its “Woodland” lineup.
Although it already sells Woodland versions of the RAV4, Sienna, bZ, and most recently, the Grand Highlander, Toyota said the new family of concept vehicles is “designed for drivers who see adventure not as a destination, but a way of life.”
Toyota’s North American design studio, CALTY Design Research, designed the concepts to explore how some of its most popular nameplates can be used better on and off the road.
Each vehicle features Horizon Blue exterior paint, inspired by Toyota’s 1960s models, including the Stout, Crown, and Corona.
All new concepts also include an exclusive Woodland badge, plus a lift kit, large over-fenders, satin-black wheels, All-Terrain tires, two-tone paint on the roof and hood, a roof rack, and cross bars to top it off.
According to Toyota, the RAV4 Woodland Plug-In Hybrid and Sienna Woodland Concepts show how its “electrified and family-focused vehicles take on a more adventurous role.”
The electric Woodland bZ Concept “extends the Woodland theme into Toyota’s battery electric future.” Meanwhile, the Grand Highlander Woodland Concept and Crown Signia Woodland Concept bring two distinct models to the lineup, Toyota said.
The company didn’t reveal any powertrain specs or other details, but said the concepts show how capability can take many forms, including PHEV, hybrid, and battery electric.
Toyota’s new Woodland Concepts will be on display at the 2026 SEMA Show, starting on November 3.
To give you an idea, the 2027 Toyota bZ Woodland comes standard with a dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain, delivering a combined 375 horsepower. That’s an extra 37 hp compared to the standard bZ with AWD.
The bZ Woodland also adds off-road capabilities with 8.3″ of ground clearance and the ability to tow up to 3,500 lbs.
Other rugged upgrades include All-Terrain tires, black side molding, roof rails, and black wheel arch cladding.
The 2027 Toyota bZ Woodland is available in Base and Premium trims, starting at $45,380, or over $10,000 more than the standard bZ.
